lessons.title: The Most Merciful Taught the Book
lessons.intro: Learn how the Qur’an introduces Allah: first with mercy, then in four short ayat that describe Him. You will also learn how a Muslim comes to know Allah in the first place.

steps.title: Start with who He is
body: Most lessons begin with rules. This course begins with a person to know: Allah. Rules make more sense once you know who is asking.

How can anyone know what the Creator is like? We cannot work it out from the outside. So Muslims take what Allah says about Himself in the Qur’an, and what the Prophet ﷺ taught about Him in authentic hadith. What a Muslim holds in the heart as true about Allah is called aqeedah (creed).
We begin with Surah Ar-Rahman. It opens with a single word.

steps.title: The opening of Surah Ar-Rahman
steps.note: Read one word at a time. The first word is a name of Allah: Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful. After it come three things He did.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Mercy first, and the first gift is guidance
body: Before the surah says anything else, it calls Allah Ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful. Then it lists what His mercy did: He taught the Qur’an, He created man, and He taught man bayan, which means clear speech. Al-Hasan al-Basri explained bayan as eloquent speech.
Ibn Kathir explains these ayat as Allah reminding people of His favours and His mercy: He sent down the Qur’an and made it easy to learn and to understand.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: The meaning of 55:1-4 is summarised from Tafsir Ibn Kathir (English text in the spa5k tafsir archive). Please confirm the wording.

steps.title: Notice the order
body: Read the four ayat again. Teaching the Qur’an is named before the creation of man. One way to take this: the Giver of life is also the Giver of guidance, and the guidance is named first.
This is a reflection to think about, not a ruling. The ayat do not explain the order.
steps.label: [Reflection]

steps.title: A second portrait: Surah Al-Ikhlas
steps.note: Four short ayat. Say each one slowly. Together they answer the question: who is Allah?
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Listen to Surah Al-Ikhlas
steps.note: Listen to each ayah, then say it aloud in the pause. The reciter’s name is shown on the player.

steps.title: What the four ayat say
body: Ibn Kathir explains each part. Ahad means the One, the Single, with no peer, no helper and no rival. As-Samad: Ibn Abbas said it means the One whom all creation depends on for their needs and requests. “He neither begets nor is born” means Allah has no child, no parent and no spouse. The last ayah says that nothing is equal to Him or like Him.
bullets: Ahad: He is One, with no partner.
As-Samad: everyone needs Him; He needs no one.
He has no parents and no children.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: Explanation of Ahad, As-Samad and kufuwan from Tafsir Ibn Kathir (including the report from Ibn Abbas). Please confirm.

steps.title: The man who loved this surah
body: The Prophet ﷺ sent a man to lead a small army. In every prayer, he ended his recitation with Surah Al-Ikhlas. When they came back, the others told the Prophet ﷺ, who said: ask him why he does this.
The man said: because it describes Ar-Rahman, and I love to recite it. The Prophet ﷺ said: tell him that Allah loves him.

In another report, the Prophet ﷺ said that Surah Al-Ikhlas is equal to one third of the Qur’an (Bukhari 5013). Scholars explain this as being about its weight in meaning, because it is so complete about who Allah is. It does not mean you can recite it three times and skip the rest of the Qur’an.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.review: The last sentence (what “a third of the Qur’an” means) is the common explanation, worded by the app author. Please confirm.

steps.title: How to learn about Allah safely
steps.intro: A simple method for building a correct picture of Allah.

steps.text: Start with what Allah said about Himself.
steps.detail: The Qur’an first. Read ayat like the ones in this lesson with their meaning.

steps.text: Add what the Prophet ﷺ taught about Him.
steps.detail: Only from authentic hadith. This app always shows the source, so you can check it.

steps.text: Do not picture Him, and do not compare Him to anything He made.
steps.detail: The Qur’an says there is nothing like Him (42:11) and that nothing is equal to Him (112:4).

steps.text: When a question troubles you, ask.
steps.detail: Ask a teacher you trust, or ask Hadi, who shows his sources. Doubts are not a sin; leaving them unanswered is what hurts.

steps.text: Let it change what you do.
steps.detail: Knowing Allah is meant to change how you pray, how you treat people and what you hope for.

mistakes: Making up a picture of Allah because it feels right.
Taking a belief from a video or a rumour without a source.
Thinking you have to understand everything before you start.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: A practical method for learning aqeedah, worded by the app author. Please confirm that nothing here goes against any of the Sunni schools of creed (Athari, Ashari, Maturidi).

items.q: Ibn Abbas explained As-Samad as the One…

options.text: who is hidden from creation
options.reteach: No. As-Samad is about creation needing Him, not about being hidden.

options.text: who rests after creating
options.reteach: No. Allah is never tired (you will see this in Ayat al-Kursi). As-Samad means the One everyone depends on.

options.text: whom all creation depends on for their needs

items.explain: As-Samad: everyone needs Him, and He needs no one (Ibn Kathir, quoting Ibn Abbas).

items.q: What does “He neither begets nor is born” teach about Allah?

options.text: Allah is one of several gods
options.reteach: No. The surah begins by saying He is One, and ends by saying nothing is equal to Him.

options.text: Allah has no parents and no children
Allah is like a very powerful human
options.reteach: No. The last ayah says there is nothing equal to Him.

items.explain: Allah has no parent and no child. He is not like His creation.

items.q: What would you tell your friend?

options.text: We do not picture Him. Nothing is like Him, so we learn about Him from what He told us.
Yes, picture whatever helps you feel close to Him.
options.reteach: The Qur’an teaches that nothing is like Him and nothing is equal to Him, so a picture will always be wrong.

options.text: Yes, but picture the strongest king you can imagine.
options.reteach: No. Nothing is like Him, not even the strongest king. We learn about Him from what He said.

items.explain: Nothing is equal to Him (112:4) and there is nothing like Him (42:11).
items.scenario: A friend says: I imagine God as a very old man sitting on a cloud. Is that what Muslims believe?

items.q: Why did the Prophet ﷺ say Allah loved the man who ended his prayers with Surah Al-Ikhlas?

options.text: Because he recited it the loudest
options.reteach: No. The report says nothing about loudness. The man said he loved it because it describes Ar-Rahman.

options.text: The man loved it because it describes Ar-Rahman
Because he led the army
options.reteach: No. The reason was his love for the surah and what it says about Allah.

items.explain: The man loved reciting it because it describes Ar-Rahman. The Prophet ﷺ said: tell him that Allah loves him.

items.q: Where does a Muslim take what he or she believes about Allah from?

options.text: From what Allah says about Himself in the Qur’an and from authentic hadith
From what feels right to each person
options.reteach: No. We cannot work out from the outside what Allah is like. We take it from what He told us.

options.text: From what most people around us believe
options.reteach: No. A belief about Allah needs a source, not a crowd.

items.explain: Beliefs about Allah come from the Qur’an and authentic hadith, which this app always shows with their source.

options.text: ahad
samad

options.text: rahmaan
options.reteach: Ar-Rahman is the first word of Surah 55. In Al-Ikhlas the missing word means One.

items.explain: Qul huwal-laahu ahad: Say, He is Allah, One.

lessons.title: No Slumber, No Sleep
lessons.intro: Learn Ayat al-Kursi: what its ten statements say about Allah, why the Prophet ﷺ called it the greatest ayah, and how to say it before you sleep.

steps.title: The greatest ayah
body: The Prophet ﷺ asked his Companion Ubayy ibn Ka’b which ayah in the Book of Allah is the greatest. Ubayy first said that Allah and His Messenger know best. When he was asked again, he named the ayah that begins “Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Eternal.” The Prophet ﷺ struck him on the chest and said: may knowledge be pleasant for you.
That ayah is Ayat al-Kursi, because it mentions Allah’s Kursi. It is ayah 255 of Surah Al-Baqarah.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Ayat al-Kursi
steps.note: Read it one word at a time. Under each Arabic word you will see how it sounds and what it means. Do not worry about getting all of it today; the next cards break it into parts.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Listen to Ayat al-Kursi
steps.note: Listen once all the way through. Then listen again and say it with the reciter, a few words at a time.

steps.title: Parts 1 and 2: who He is
body: Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as ten statements. The first is: Allah, there is no god but Him. He alone is the Lord of all creation.
The second is Al-Hayy Al-Qayyum. Al-Hayy: the Ever-Living, who never dies. Al-Qayyum: the One who sustains everyone and everything. All creation depends on Him, and He depends on nothing He created.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.review: Plain-words summary of the first two of the ten statements in Tafsir Ibn Kathir. Please confirm.

steps.title: Part 3: no drowsiness, no sleep
body: Sinah is drowsiness, the first edge of sleep. Nawm is full sleep. The ayah says neither of them overtakes Allah. Ibn Kathir notes that sleep is stronger than drowsiness, so the ayah removes the small weakness first and then the large one.
The Prophet ﷺ taught the same: Allah does not sleep, and it does not suit Him to sleep (Muslim 179).
So there is no moment when the world is unwatched. He knows everything at every moment.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur’an 2:255; Muslim 179; Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur’an 2:255

steps.title: Parts 4 and 5: He owns it all, and nobody speaks for another without His leave
body: To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Everyone in them is His servant.
Then the ayah asks a question: who can intercede with Him, except by His permission? Nobody. Even the angels and the prophets can speak for someone only if He allows it.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.source: Qur’an 2:255; Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur’an 2:255

steps.title: Parts 6 to 10: knowledge, the Kursi, and the end of the ayah
body: He knows what is before people and what is behind them. People can know only what He lets them know.

His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth. Ibn Kathir reports Ibn Abbas as saying that the Kursi is the footstool, and that no one can truly measure the Throne. Scholars do not describe more than what is reported.
Looking after the heavens and the earth does not tire Him. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Qur’an 2:255; Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur’an 2:255
steps.review: The explanation of Kursi (report from Ibn Abbas that it is the footstool) is from Tafsir Ibn Kathir. Scholars of different schools of creed explain such descriptions differently. Please confirm the wording.

steps.title: Abu Hurayrah and the visitor
body: The Prophet ﷺ put Abu Hurayrah in charge of looking after the Ramadan charity food. For three nights a visitor came and took handfuls. Each night he said he was poor, and Abu Hurayrah let him go. On the third night, the visitor said: I will teach you words that will benefit you. When you go to bed, recite Ayat al-Kursi from the beginning to the end. A guard from Allah will stay with you, and no devil will come near you until morning.
In the morning the Prophet ﷺ said: he told you the truth, though he is a liar. He then told Abu Hurayrah that the visitor was Shaytan.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: How to recite it before you sleep
steps.intro: A short habit with a source.

steps.detail: The hadith says to recite it when you go to your bed.
The report says to recite it from the beginning to the end. If you cannot yet say it by heart, read it from this lesson.

steps.text: Say it slowly, knowing what it means.
steps.detail: It is remembrance of who Allah is. The meaning is what protects the heart.
Trust that He is the One who does not sleep.

mistakes: Treating it like a lucky charm without knowing what it says.
Skipping the second half because it is harder to remember.
steps.label: [Established]

options.text: It only counts if you do not know the meaning
options.reteach: No. The meaning matters. It is remembrance of who Allah is.

options.text: The report says to recite the whole ayah, from beginning to end

items.explain: The report says to recite Ayat al-Kursi from the beginning to the end.

items.q: Which of these tells us Allah does not need rest?

options.text: The Kursi is small
options.reteach: No. The ayah says His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth.

options.text: People look after the heavens
options.reteach: No. The ayah says He looks after them, and that it does not tire Him.

options.text: Looking after the heavens and the earth does not tire Him

items.explain: And their preservation tires Him not (2:255).

lessons.title: The Attribute We Say Most
lessons.intro: Learn the two names of mercy in the basmala, what scholars say separates them, and the hadith about Allah’s mercy that every beginner should hear.

steps.title: The basmala
steps.note: You say this at the start of most things. Look at the last two words: both come from the word for mercy.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Mercy, named twice
body: Of all the things Allah could put first, the basmala names mercy, and names it twice: Ar-Rahman and Ar-Raheem. The basmala opens every surah of the Qur’an except Surah At-Tawbah (Surah 9).
Both names come from rahmah, mercy. So you say the words of mercy again and again every day, in every prayer.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.review: The statement that every surah except At-Tawbah opens with the basmala is a standard fact about the Qur’anic text; please confirm.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two?
body: Ibn Kathir says Ar-Rahman has more meanings of mercy than Ar-Raheem. He quotes Abu Ali al-Farisi: Ar-Rahman, a name only for Allah, covers every kind of mercy that Allah has. Ar-Raheem is the mercy that reaches the believers, as the Qur’an says (33:43) that He is ever Raheem to the believers.
Another early scholar, al-Azrami, is quoted as saying: He is Ar-Rahman with all of creation and Ar-Raheem with the believers.
A simple way to remember it: Ar-Rahman is mercy that reaches everyone. Ar-Raheem is mercy that reaches the believers in a special way.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur’an 1:1; Qur’an 33:43
steps.review: Summary of the difference between Ar-Rahman and Ar-Raheem from Tafsir Ibn Kathir (Abu Ali al-Farisi, al-Azrami). The last “simple way to remember” sentence is the app author’s. Scholars hold other views too. Please confirm.

steps.title: The hadith about His mercy
steps.note: The Prophet ﷺ said that when Allah created creation, He wrote in His Book, which is with Him on the Throne: my mercy overcomes my anger.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Allah is more merciful than a mother
body: Some captives were brought to the Prophet ﷺ. Among them was a woman who was looking for her baby. When she found a child among the captives she held it to her chest and nursed it.

The Prophet ﷺ asked his Companions: do you think this woman would throw her child in the fire? They said: no, not if she could help it. He said: Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: One part of a hundred
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah made mercy in one hundred parts. He kept ninety-nine with Him and sent down one part to the earth. Because of that one part, creatures are kind to each other. Even a horse lifts its hoof from its baby so it does not hurt it.
Think of the best kindness you have ever received. That was one part of a hundred.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Using the names in your day
steps.intro: Four small ways to turn this lesson into a habit.

steps.detail: Before you eat, start a task or open the Qur’an. Think: I am beginning with the Most Merciful.

steps.text: When you feel you have failed, name His mercy.
steps.detail: Say: Ya Rahman, Ya Raheem. You are speaking to the One whose mercy overcomes His anger.
The Prophet ﷺ said that the one part of mercy is why creatures are kind to each other. Be a place where it lands.

steps.text: Do not use mercy as an excuse.
steps.detail: Knowing He is merciful is meant to make you turn to Him more, not less.

body: Ahsaaha, the word translated “counts them”, has been explained by scholars as: counting them, memorising them, understanding what they mean, and acting on them. The fullest sense is all four.
Many scholars, including al-Nawawi in his commentary on Muslim, say the hadith does not mean Allah has only ninety-nine names. The number is the group the Prophet ﷺ promised a reward for learning.

The numbered list many Muslims learn comes from a hadith in Tirmidhi (3507). Shakir, al-Albani and Zubair Ali Zai all graded that hadith as weak (daif). Because of this, scholars have compiled the names from the Qur’an and sound hadith, and their lists differ a little.

lessons.title: One Message, Many Messengers
lessons.intro: Learn why Muslims say Islam is not a new religion: every prophet brought the same call, and the Qur’an says so in its own words.

steps.title: Is Islam a new religion?
body: A common question: Islam started with Muhammad ﷺ about 1,400 years ago, so how can it be the religion of Ibrahim or Musa?
The Qur’an answers this directly. It says Allah sent a messenger to every nation, and that every messenger brought the same first message: worship Allah alone.
This lesson looks at what stays the same from one prophet to the next, and what changes.

steps.title: Two ayat on the one message
steps.note: Read these slowly. In the first, Allah sends a messenger to every nation. In the second, every messenger is told that there is no god but Allah.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: What the word Islam means
body: Islam means submitting to Allah. Because of this, the Qur’an can say that the religion with Allah is Islam (3:19), and that Ibrahim was a Muslim, one who submits to Allah (3:67). It also tells believers to say that they believe in what was sent to all the prophets and make no difference between them (2:136).
So when a Muslim says Islam is the religion of every prophet, they mean this: the core message, worship Allah alone, has always been the same.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The Prophet ﷺ on the prophets
steps.note: The Prophet ﷺ compared the prophets to brothers from one father with different mothers. The father stands for the one religion. The mothers stand for the different laws.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: What stays the same, and what changes
body: What stays the same: believing in Allah alone, in the angels, the books, the messengers and the Last Day, and living as a servant of Allah.

What can change: the detailed laws. The Qur’an says that to each community Allah gave a law and a way (5:48). It also says that Isa came to make lawful some of what had been forbidden to his people (3:50).
This is why a Muslim does not see the Qur’an as cancelling the earlier prophets. It confirms what came before it and is the last word (5:48).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: A chain of messengers
body: The Qur’an says Allah chose Adam and Nuh and the family of Ibrahim over the worlds (3:33). It then says He sent Nuh and Ibrahim and placed prophethood and scripture among their descendants (57:26). After the earlier messengers, He sent Isa, the son of Maryam (5:46). The Qur’an ends the line with Muhammad, the last of the prophets (33:40).
So the order of the main names is: Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa, and then Muhammad ﷺ. Many other prophets came between them.
steps.label: [Established]
steps.review: The order Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa, Muhammad is the commonly taught order. Musa is placed by the order of the books (the Torah before the Gospel); please confirm the wording.

lessons.title: Believing in the Unseen
lessons.intro: Learn what the unseen is, how the hadith of Jibril lists the six pillars of faith, and what the angels and the decree (qadar) mean for daily life.

steps.title: Belief in the unseen
body: The Qur’an opens with a guidance for those who are mindful of Allah, and the first thing it says about them is that they believe in the unseen (2:3). The unseen (ghayb) is whatever our senses cannot reach: Allah, the angels, the Last Day.
The Qur’an says that the keys of the unseen are with Allah, and no one knows them but Him (6:59). He shares some of it with messengers (72:26-27).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The ayah in Arabic
steps.note: Read one word at a time. The third word is the unseen.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The visitor in white
body: One day a man in very white clothes, with very black hair, came to the Prophet ﷺ while he sat with his Companions. No one knew him, and he showed no sign of travel. He sat close to the Prophet ﷺ and asked about Islam, about faith, and about ihsan.
After the man left, the Prophet ﷺ told Umar that it was Jibril, who had come to teach them their religion. This is the hadith of Jibril. It is the clearest short summary of faith.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The six pillars of faith
steps.note: This is the answer given in the hadith. Read the six parts: Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The angels
body: The angels are creatures of Allah made from light, as the Prophet ﷺ taught (Muslim 2996). The Qur’an says they do what they are commanded and do not disobey (66:6). They have wings (35:1) and they are honoured servants, not children of Allah (21:26-27).
The Qur’an also says two angels record what a person does (82:10-12). Believing in them is part of faith. It reminds us that we are always watched over and that our deeds are kept.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The decree (qadar)
body: The last pillar is belief in qadar, the decree of Allah. The Qur’an says that Allah created everything with a measure (54:49), and that no disaster strikes except what is written before it happens (57:22).

It also says that people choose: whoever wills may take a way to his Lord (76:29). Then it adds that we do not will except what Allah wills (76:30). Muslims hold both together: Allah knows and decreed all things, and people are responsible for their choices.

The Prophet ﷺ gave practical advice: work for what helps you and ask Allah for help. If something goes wrong, do not say “if I had done that, it would not have happened”. Say: this is the decree of Allah, and what He willed He did. The word “if” opens the door to Shaytan (Muslim 2664).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: How the schools explain choice and decree
steps.intro: Sunni scholars agree on both ideas. They differ in how they explain how the two fit together.
steps.agree: All three affirm that Allah knows and decreed everything, that people choose, and that people are responsible.

rows.name: Ashari
rows.text: Allah creates every action, and a person “acquires” it (kasb) by choosing. Both the decree and human responsibility are real.

rows.name: Maturidi
rows.text: Allah decreed all things and gives people real ability to choose. People are held responsible for that choice.

rows.name: Athari (hadith tradition)
rows.text: Affirm what the Qur’an and hadith say about decree and choice, and refrain from going deeper into how they fit together.

steps.closing: This is a high-level summary for beginners. Ask a teacher for more.

steps.title: Believing in all of them
body: Believing in the messengers is the fourth pillar of faith. A Muslim believes in all of them and makes no difference between them in faith (2:285). To deny one is to deny the message.

The Qur’an names some prophets and says there are others it has not told us about (4:164; 40:78). So we believe in all, and we speak with certainty only about the ones the Qur’an and the authentic hadith name.

steps.title: How many prophets are named?
body: Scholars commonly say that twenty-five prophets are named in the Qur’an. Some counts differ: for example, scholars differ about Dhul-Kifl. The Qur’an itself does not give a number.
There is no need to memorise a count. What matters is that the Qur’an says there were many more than the ones it names (40:78).

steps.title: Ibrahim looks for his Lord
body: The Qur’an tells how Ibrahim spoke to his people about the star, the moon and the sun. At night he saw a star and said: this is my lord. When it set, he said that he did not love what disappears. He did the same with the moon and then the sun. Each one set (6:76-78).
Then he said to his people that he was free of what they joined with Allah, and that he turned his face to the One who made the heavens and the earth (6:79).

Many scholars explain that Ibrahim was showing his people, step by step, that something which sets cannot be a lord. The ayat say that this was the argument Allah gave to Ibrahim against his people (6:83).
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Qur’an 6:76-79; Qur’an 6:83; Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur’an 6:76-79

lessons.title: He Is With You
lessons.intro: Learn three ways the Qur’an says Allah is with us: in knowledge, in help, and in answering when we call. See how Abu Bakr and the Prophet ﷺ lived it in the cave.

steps.title: Three ways Allah is “with” you
body: The Qur’an often says that Allah is with people. Scholars explain that this is used in more than one way. One way is general: He is with everyone by His knowledge, hearing and sight. Another is special: He is with the believers by His help and support. A third is nearness to the one who calls on Him.
None of this means that Allah is mixed with His creation or that He needs a place. It means He knows us, helps us and answers us.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur’an 57:4; Qur’an 58:7
steps.review: The grouping into general and special “withness” is a common way scholars explain these ayat. Please confirm the wording and that it does not go beyond Ibn Kathir.

steps.title: With everyone: He knows
steps.note: The ayah says He created the heavens and the earth, that He knows all that goes in and out, and that He is with you wherever you are. The ayah ends by saying He sees what you do. Read the last part carefully.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: With the believers: He helps
body: To Musa and Harun, Allah said: do not fear, I am with you both; I hear and I see (20:46). To the believers He says that He is with the patient (2:153).
Here “with” means help, support and care. It is why a believer in trouble can say, with Musa, that Allah is near.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: In the cave
body: When the Prophet ﷺ left Makkah, he and Abu Bakr hid in a cave. The pursuers came close. Abu Bakr said: if one of them looks under his feet, he will see us.

The Prophet ﷺ replied: Abu Bakr, what do you think of two, the third of whom is Allah? (Bukhari 3653). The Qur’an describes the same moment: the Prophet ﷺ told his companion not to grieve because Allah is with us, and Allah sent down calm on him (9:40).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Near to the one who asks
steps.note: When His servants ask about Him, He says He is near and answers the one who calls. Say the ayah slowly, then think of one thing you would ask for.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Closer than the vein
body: The Qur’an says that Allah created man and knows what his soul whispers to him, and that He is closer than the jugular vein (50:16). Ibn Kathir explains that the nearness here refers to His angels, who are closer to a person than his own vein, and he rejects reading “We” as only “Our knowledge”. Other scholars read it as nearness in knowledge.
Either way, nothing about you is hidden from Him.
steps.label: [Interpretive]
steps.source: Qur’an 50:16; Tafsir Ibn Kathir on Qur’an 50:16
steps.review: Ibn Kathir reads the nearness in 50:16 as the angels; others read it as knowledge. Please confirm the wording and that the dispute is stated fairly.

steps.title: How the schools explain “with you”
steps.intro: Sunni scholars agree that Allah is not mixed with His creation and that nothing is like Him. They differ in how they explain such words.
steps.agree: All agree: He is not like His creation, He is not mixed with it, and He knows and hears us.

rows.name: Athari
rows.text: Affirm the words as Allah said them: He is with us, and He is above the Throne, in a way that suits Him. Do not ask how, and do not compare Him to anything.

rows.name: Ashari and Maturidi
rows.text: Being with us means His knowledge, power, help and care. He is not in any place, and He is not mixed with creation.

steps.closing: This is a short summary for beginners. Ask a teacher for more.

lessons.title: The Balance
lessons.intro: Learn what the Qur’an says about the scales on the Day of Judgment, why no one will be wronged, and what this means for how we treat one another now.

steps.title: A balance that is fair
body: On the Day of Judgment, the Qur’an says, Allah places scales of justice and no soul is wronged at all (21:47). Even something as small as an atom’s weight is counted (99:7-8; 4:40).
This is good news for the person who was treated unjustly and could not get justice in life. It is a warning for the one who wronged others.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: The scales
steps.note: Read slowly. The ayah says no soul will be wronged and that even a mustard seed’s weight will be brought forth.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Do not break the balance
steps.note: Surah Ar-Rahman says Allah set the balance and tells us not to transgress in it. It tells us to weigh with justice and not to make the balance fall short.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: A hadith qudsi on injustice
steps.note: Allah says that He made injustice forbidden for Himself and forbidden between people. This is a hadith qudsi, a saying where the Prophet ﷺ reports Allah’s own words.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Rights will be returned
body: The Prophet ﷺ said that rights will be returned to their owners on the Day of Resurrection, even the hornless sheep will take its right from the horned one (Muslim 2582).

He also taught: if a man has wronged another in his honour or anything else, he should seek forgiveness from him now, before a day when there is no money, only good deeds. Good deeds are taken from the wrongdoer, and if he has none, the sins of the wronged are placed on him (Bukhari 2449).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Who is bankrupt?
body: The Prophet ﷺ asked the Companions: do you know who is bankrupt? They said: the one with no money. He said: the bankrupt person of my community comes on the Day of Resurrection with prayer, fasting and zakat, but he has insulted this one, slandered that one, taken the money of another, shed blood and hit someone. His good deeds are given to those he wronged. If they run out, their sins are put on him, and he is thrown into the Fire (Muslim 2581).
steps.label: [Established]

steps.title: Justice in daily life
body: The Qur’an tells believers to stand firm for Allah as witnesses of justice, and not to let hatred of a people stop them from being just (5:8). It warns those who cheat when they weigh and measure (83:1-3).
This means that justice is not just for courts. It is how we weigh in a shop, how we treat a person we dislike, and how we speak about someone who is not there.
steps.label: [Established]

steps.intro: If you wronged someone, the hadith says to put it right now.

steps.detail: Be honest with yourself. Did you take, insult or spread something about someone?
Repent sincerely and promise not to repeat it.
Return the money, or ask the person for what would make it right.
Do it now, as the Prophet ﷺ advised, before the day when only deeds count.

lessons.title: A Creed You Can Carry
lessons.intro: Bring the course together: who Allah is, what we believe about the unseen, the prophets, His nearness and His justice, in a form you can say in a few lines.

steps.title: What you now hold
body: This course moved from Allah’s mercy and His names, to the unseen, to the prophets, to His nearness and justice. These are not separate ideas. They fit together: the One who is Merciful sent messengers; He is near; and He is just.
This lesson gathers them into a short creed you can carry.

steps.title: Your creed in six lines
body: Allah is One, with no partner, and nothing is like Him (112:1-4).
He is Merciful, and His mercy overcomes His anger (Bukhari 7404).
He has most beautiful names, and we know Him by them (7:180).
He sent messengers to every nation with one message; Muhammad ﷺ is the last (33:40).
We believe in the unseen: angels, books, the Last Day and the decree (Muslim 8).
He is near, He sees us, and He is just: no soul will be wronged (21:47).

steps.title: A creed is meant to change you
body: The Prophet ﷺ did not teach belief as a list to memorise. In the hadith of Jibril, faith, Islam and ihsan come together: what you believe, what you do, and how you do it.
When you know that He is merciful, you hope. When you know He is just, you give people their rights. When you know He sees you, you act the same in private as in public.
